attributes.nuance_translation: A grammar point that expresses lists of actions that occur in no particular order.

attributes.body:
In Japanese, たり is a 'conjunction particle' that is used in exactly the same way as て. However, instead of having the nuance of 'then', or 'and', it has the nuance of 'and things like'. Basically, it is used for listing sequences of events that do not happen in a specific order.

The last たり in any sequence should be followed by a form of する (for example, した for past tense).

From these examples we can see that たり will sometimes be said as だり. This happens with the same verbs that usually use だ for past tense (like 読（よ）んだ), or で for the て form ( like 泳（およ）いで). This will not change the meaning at all, and is only to help make the words easier to say.

To summarize, the difference between て form, and たり is as follows.

Events in order - I did (A) て, (B) て, (C) て, (D) た.

Events in no specific order - I did (D) たり, (B) たり, (A) たり, (C) たりした.

たり is frequently used when there is only one verb in the sentence. This just means that the speaker did 'things like (A)', without specifically listing anything else.

Caution

In cases where a する verb is the last verb in a particular sequence, たり will often be omitted.

Fun Fact

Sometimes sentences will end with たりして, which is たり combined with the て form of する. たりして is used at the end of a sentence to express uncertainty, ambiguity, or that something that is unlikely may actually be true. It can also be used in a joking way.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.description: Expressing multiple actions or states using 「～たりする」

attributes.body: Both たり～たりする and とか～とか are used to give examples of actions, similar to the English '(doing) things like A and B.' The key difference is how they attach to words. たり is made by adding り to the た (past tense) of a verb, while とか follows the dictionary form. Also, とか can follow nouns directly, while たり requires だ to become だったり.

second_relatable.title: とか～とか
second_relatable.meaning: Among other things, For example, Such as

attributes.body: Both たり～たりする and やら～やら list examples of actions, like saying 'doing things like A and B' in English. たり is more neutral, while やら adds a nuance of uncertainty or a wider, less-defined range, suggesting the speaker is listing just some of many possible actions or things.

first_relatable.title: やら～やら
first_relatable.meaning: Whether or, Things like, And … so on

attributes.body: Both たり～たりする and ～なり～なり list example actions, like 'doing things like A and B.' たり is a neutral, commonly used pattern in casual speech. In contrast, なり～なり is more formal and carries a stronger nuance that the examples are just possibilities, often implying that the speaker doesn't care which one is chosen.

Both たり～たりする and や can be used to provide or list examples, similar to the English 'things like A and B.' The main difference is that たり can only be used with verbs, adjectives, or noun phrases, while や can only be used to list nouns. Note that both grammar points suggest that the speaker is listing just some of many possible actions or things.
